articleEn: On 25 November 1915, in Berlin, Albert Einstein presented his updated field equations to the Prussian Academy of Sciences. It was a major turning point in physics. But these equations were not his first answer. In October 1915 Einstein had already published another version, and it later had to be corrected. So why was that first version wrong, and why did Einstein have to go back to the drawing board to fix it?

A second question follows: what does the equation actually say? And where does the famous mathematician David Hilbert fit into the story? The tale also includes a solar eclipse in 1919, which made Einstein famous around the world. And from the solutions of these same equations came the prediction of black holes, about which Einstein himself was doubtful.

So let's follow this journey from the beginning. First we step into Newton's world, where gravity was seen as a force. We will also see how Einstein, working in a patent office, moved from one simple idea toward changing our understanding of space and time. Get ready, because this story has mistakes, failed expeditions and a surprising success.

articleEn: The story begins with Newton. His law of universal gravitation was considered the correct account of gravity for more than two hundred years. In this theory gravity was a force pulling two massive objects toward each other, though Newton himself was not comfortable with the nature of that force. Within a century, careful astronomical observations showed some differences between theory and observation that could not be explained. These included small anomalies in the orbits of Mercury and other planets. Newton's theory could not account for them. In 1905 Henri Poincare proposed the first relativistic theory of gravity, in which gravity was transmitted by gravitational waves traveling at the speed of light.

Now we come to Einstein. He later explained that he was bothered by the way special relativity favored inertial motion. He thought a better theory would not favor any particular state of motion from the start. In 1907 Einstein was still working at the patent office. Then he had the idea he called his happiest thought: that the principle of relativity could be extended to gravitational fields, bringing gravity within the same principle.

That same year he wrote an article on acceleration, published in 1908. In it he argued that free fall is really inertial motion, so the principles of special relativity apply to a freely falling observer. Today this argument is called the equivalence principle. In the same article Einstein also predicted gravitational time dilation, the effect of gravity on time.

In 1911 Einstein wrote another paper. It described a box moving with uniform acceleration, away from any gravitational field. Einstein said such a box cannot be distinguished from a box sitting at rest in a constant gravitational field. From this he concluded that in a box accelerating upward, clocks at the top would run faster than clocks at the bottom. In other words, the rate of time in a gravitational field depends on your position, and to a first approximation the difference is proportional to the gravitational potential.

This paper also made another major prediction: massive objects such as the Sun or Jupiter bend light. By Einstein's calculation the deflection was 0.83 arcseconds. He asked astronomers to test the prediction by looking at stars near the Sun during an eclipse.

articleEn: Another thought experiment pushed Einstein toward geometry. It was the picture of a rotating disk, a form of what is called the Ehrenfest paradox. Imagine an observer standing on a spinning turntable and doing experiments there. What would the observer find? Einstein concluded that the observer would find the ratio of a circle's circumference to its radius to be greater than 2π, which differs from what Euclidean geometry expects. The reason is that the radius is measured with a ruler that does not shrink, while according to special relativity the ruler measuring the circumference does contract.

Einstein believed that the laws of physics are local, that is, described by local fields. What was the next step in this thinking? The result was striking: spacetime can be curved locally. Einstein now needed a language in which curved space could be described.

In 1912 Einstein returned to Switzerland as a professor at his alma mater, ETH Zurich. The city proved an important turning point in the story. Upon arriving he met his old ETH classmate Marcel Grossmann, who was now a professor of mathematics. Grossmann introduced him to Riemannian geometry and, more generally, differential geometry, and this geometry became the language of the theory. On the advice of the Italian mathematician Tullio Levi-Civita, Einstein began to explore general covariance, which essentially means the use of tensors.

In 1913 Einstein abandoned this approach on the basis of the hole argument, because in his view it was inconsistent. Then through much of 1914 and 1915 he tried to build the field equations by another route. But that route also proved inconsistent. So what path was left? The answer was hidden in the old one. Einstein looked again at general covariance and discovered that the hole argument itself was wrong. The very argument that made him give up covariance turned out to be flawed, and general covariance was tenable. Once this became clear, Einstein quickly completed the field equations, the same equations that carry his name today.

One point is important here: the theory did not come together in a single moment. It was built over many years of wrong turns and retreats. According to general relativity, gravity is the result of matter distorting the structure of spacetime, which in turn affects the inertial motion of other matter.

articleEn: Now the question was how to test Einstein's prediction. The answer was in the sky, during a solar eclipse, when stars become visible in the daytime. In October 1911 the German astronomer Erwin Freundlich contacted Charles Perrine. The question was whether old eclipse photographs could confirm Einstein's prediction. Perrine was director of the National Observatory in Cordoba, Argentina. He had taken part in four eclipse campaigns at Lick Observatory, in 1900, 1901, 1905 and 1908. But Perrine was not sure the old eclipse photographs would be of any use.

In 1912 Freundlich asked whether he would include a light deflection observation in his expedition. That eclipse took place in Brazil on 10 October 1912. W. W. Campbell, director of Lick Observatory, lent Perrine a special long-focus camera lens. The Cordoba team was the only expedition that built special equipment for observing light deflection. Everything was ready, but then the sky did not cooperate. All the expeditions faced pouring rain and no observation was possible. Even so, Perrine was the first astronomer to make a proper attempt.

Two years later three teams were ready: Freundlich, Campbell and Perrine. The destination was Crimea in the Russian Empire, where an eclipse was due on 21 August 1914. But the First World War had begun in July, and on 1 August Germany declared war on Russia. The German astronomers either had to return home or were arrested by the Russians. American and Argentine astronomers were not taken into custody. But clouds took that chance away as well. Perrine's photographs were not clear enough to prove Einstein's prediction, though they were the first photographs of this kind of attempt.

History took a strange turn here, because these failures saved Einstein. In 1911 he had calculated a deflection of only 0.83 arcseconds. That value was too small by half, because the approximation he used does not hold for things moving near the speed of light. If clear results had come in 1912 or 1914, Einstein's 1911 prediction might have turned out wrong and damaged his reputation. The weather gave him time.

In 1915, when the complete theory was ready, Einstein corrected his mistake and gave the correct value for a star at the Sun's edge as 1.75 arcseconds. Meanwhile, in 1917 Mount Wilson Observatory published an analysis of the solar spectrum in which gravitational redshift was not seen. That was not good news for Einstein. In 1918 Lick Observatory also announced that it had disproved Einstein's prediction, but its results were never published. In the 1918 eclipse the American effort was left incomplete, with clouds in one place and the right equipment missing in another. All eyes were now on 1919.

articleEn: In October 1915 Einstein published his field equations. Their form was surprisingly simple: Rμν equals κ Tμν. Here Rμν is the Ricci tensor, a measure of spacetime curvature. Tμν is the energy-momentum tensor, and κ is Einstein's gravitational constant. In plain words, geometry stood on one side and matter and energy on the other. The equation told how matter bends spacetime.

It also showed a major success. These equations predicted the non-Newtonian perihelion precession of Mercury's orbit, and Einstein was extremely excited. Mercury was the planet whose orbit could not be fully understood with Newton's gravity. There was a small but stubborn gap between observation and theory, which is why Einstein was so happy. Later, this same precession of Mercury became the first evidence in favor of general relativity.

But the story does not end there. It soon became clear that the equations hid a deep flaw, tied to the conservation of energy and momentum. A basic principle of physics is that energy and momentum are conserved locally. That is, in any place you look, stress-energy does not vanish or appear from nowhere. According to the sources, this is a physical requirement. Einstein's final equations ensured that general relativity meets this condition. But the October equations did not satisfy it fully. They agreed with local conservation only if the density of mass-energy-momentum were the same throughout the entire universe.

That would mean something very odd: air, rock and empty space would all have to have the same density. Obviously the real world is not like that. Air, rock and vacuum do not have the same density. The equation clashed with observation. This inconsistency sent Einstein back to the drawing board. The equations that had thrilled him now had to be changed.

Another property of the equations is also important. They are nonlinear, meaning that adding two solutions does not give a new solution. That is why, unlike Maxwell's equations, which are linear, Einstein's equations are hard to solve. In full form they are a system of ten coupled partial differential equations. Each tensor has ten independent components, and four Bianchi identities reduce the number of independent equations from 10 to 6.

So at this point in 1915 the question in front of Einstein was clear: could an equation be found that describes curvature without breaking the law of conservation? The answer was presented on 25 November 1915 at the Prussian Academy of Sciences. But before that, another person must be mentioned: David Hilbert.

articleEn: Now David Hilbert enters the story. He was a German mathematician, and during the final year of Einstein's work on general relativity the two met and exchanged letters. Hilbert was then working on a unified field theory based on the ideas of Gustav Mie. His path was different from Einstein's. Then Hilbert derived the theory of general relativity from an elegant variational principle. This work came almost at the same time as Einstein's discovery. In other words, two minds arrived at the same theory at nearly the same time. This timing of letters and hints has given rise to many deep historical analyses. A glimpse of it survives in the equations even today: the Einstein-Hilbert action is what these equations are derived from.

Here Rμν is the Ricci curvature tensor, R is the scalar curvature, and gμν is the metric tensor of spacetime. The solutions of the equation are in fact the components of this metric. The left-hand side is called the Einstein tensor Gμν. It is a symmetric, divergenceless tensor that depends only on the metric and its first and second derivatives. One consequence of these equations is local energy-momentum conservation. That means the October flaw was now gone.

On the right-hand side is κ, the Einstein gravitational constant. Its value is 8πG divided by c to the fourth power, roughly 2.07665 times 10 to the power of minus 43 per Newton. And the most beautiful part? When gravity is weak and speeds are far below the speed of light, these equations turn into Newton's law of gravity. In other words, Newton's law is recovered as a limit of this theory. The value of the constant G is also fixed through this approximation.

These equations tell us how geometry is determined. Then, with the help of the geodesic equation, we find the paths of particles and light in this geometry. One more point: in standard units, every term on the left side has dimension L to the power of minus 2. But the real challenge was finding solutions. The solutions are spacetime metrics. Some of the exact solutions model phenomena such as rotating black holes and the expanding universe. So could anyone actually solve these difficult equations? Einstein thought not, but someone proved him wrong.

articleEn: Yes, Karl Schwarzschild did. He found an exact solution in 1915 and published it in 1916. It described a spherically symmetric spacetime around a massive object. Today it is called the Schwarzschild solution. Einstein thought these equations could not be solved at all because they are non-linear. But after this, many other exact solutions were found. The study of exact solutions is very important. From it came the prediction of black holes, and various models of the evolution of the universe were built.

Reissner found the solution for a charged, spherically symmetric object, and Nordström later rediscovered it. It is called the Reissner–Nordström solution. The black hole aspect of the Schwarzschild solution was highly controversial. Einstein himself did not believe that singularities could be real. Then in 1957, two years after Einstein's death, Martin Kruskal published a proof that the Schwarzschild solution requires black holes. In the 1960s Roy Kerr obtained the solution for a rotating massive object, called the Kerr solution. A few years later the Kerr–Newman solution was published, for a rotating and charged massive object.

Now to the whole universe. In 1922 Alexander Friedmann found a solution in which the universe can expand or contract. Then Lemaître found the solution for an expanding universe. But Einstein believed the universe was static. Since the equations did not support a static cosmology, he added the cosmological constant Λ. This produced steady-state solutions, but they were unstable. A slight perturbation would make the universe expand or contract. And the term was an ad hoc hypothesis at the time, added only to justify one result, a static universe.

Then in 1929 Edwin Hubble found evidence that the universe really is expanding. Einstein dropped Λ and called it the biggest blunder of his career. But the story did not end there. Modern astronomical observations show that the expansion of the universe is accelerating, and explaining this requires a positive value of Λ.

Another method is approximation. If the gravitational field far from a source is weak, spacetime is nearly like Minkowski space. This gives the linearized equations, and gravitational waves are studied through these linearized equations. Could the theory be tested in the sky? Yes, in 1919.

articleEn: In 1916 the war was going on, and Arthur Eddington received Einstein's papers. They had been sent to the Royal Astronomical Society by the neutral Dutch physicist Willem de Sitter. Eddington understood the importance of the theory. He gave a lecture on relativity at a meeting of the British Association and said that tests such as eclipse observations were essential. Astronomer Royal Frank Watson Dyson began planning for the May 1919 eclipse. On that day the Sun would be in front of the bright stars called the Hyades, which would make the shift easier to measure.

In 1917 conscription began in Britain. Eddington was a Quaker, and he took the position of a conscientious objector on religious grounds. In the hearings of June and July 1918, Dyson supported an exemption. He proposed that Eddington go on the eclipse expedition and test Einstein's theory. The appeal board granted a twelve-month extension. In November the Armistice came and the extension became unnecessary, but the expedition still went ahead as planned.

Two teams were formed, with two people each. Eddington and Edwin Turner Cottingham went to the island of Príncipe, while Andrew Crommelin and Charles Davidson went to the Brazilian town of Sobral. The real question was whether the deflection of light was 0.83 arcseconds or 1.75. The first value was the Newtonian one, and the second came from Einstein's complete theory.

On the morning of 29 May 1919 there was a storm and rain at Príncipe. Eddington wrote that the rain stopped at noon, and around 1.30 a glimpse of the Sun appeared. He took 16 photographs. The pictures of the Sun were good, but clouds affected the star images. In the last few plates some stars were visible. On 3 June Eddington wrote in his notebook that the one plate he had measured gave a result in agreement with Einstein.

At Sobral the Greenwich team had two telescopes, one of 13 inches and a small one of 4 inches. The eclipse lasted 5 minutes 13 seconds. The images from the large telescope were blurred, so they were left out of the final conclusion. Their deflection estimates were closer to the Newtonian prediction. The small telescope's images were the clearest. Its estimate was slightly above Einstein's prediction. According to Kennefick, without Sobral the 1919 results would have been inconclusive.

On 6 November 1919 the results were presented at a joint meeting of the Royal Society and the Royal Astronomical Society. There was huge newspaper coverage, especially in The New York Times. In this way Einstein became famous around the world. But in Belgium the results got a cold reception, because Einstein was seen as a representative of Germany.

Were the results really that strong? Around 1973 some people expressed suspicion that the analysis had been biased. But modern reanalysis shows that Eddington's analysis was correct. In 1979 a re-measurement of the Sobral plates with a modern machine also confirmed their results.

articleEn: So the story began on 25 November 1915. Einstein corrected a wrong equation, and it tied the geometry of spacetime to matter-energy. Since 1919 many observations have agreed with the theory. These include studies of binary pulsars. Radio signals passing the edge of the Sun are also included, and so is the global positioning system. In other words, GPS also shows agreement with the theory's predictions.

The visible-light eclipse measurements had a lot of uncertainty. Only in the late 1960s did radio measurements settle the matter decisively. They proved that the deflection is the full value general relativity gives, not the half value of the Newtonian calculation. Then on 14 September 2015 the Advanced LIGO team observed gravitational waves for the first time. They came from the merger of two black holes. So 100 years after the theory was published, another of its predictions was confirmed, and a century of waiting ended. Then on 10 April 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration published the first image of the supermassive black hole at the center of the galaxy Messier 87.

According to Kip Thorne, the period from about 1960 to 1975 was the golden age of black hole research. Then general relativity moved from being a curiosity into mainstream theoretical physics. The experiment was important to Karl Popper too. In his idea of falsifiability, every scientific theory needs a test that could prove it wrong. Popper called general relativity an example of good science, because the Eddington experiment could have proved it wrong, but did not.

Now the question is whether everything has been solved. No. Friends, the truth is that many questions about the field equations are still open today. For example, no complete solution is known for a spacetime with two massive bodies. For models such as binary star systems, post-Newtonian approximations are used. The other big problem is quantum mechanics. General relativity is inconsistent with it, and quantum mechanics currently does not describe gravitational attraction at microscopic scales. The speculative theory that would join the two is called quantum gravity. Examples are string theory and loop quantum gravity.

Cosmology has an important side too. The Λ term is equivalent to vacuum energy, and explaining the accelerating expansion requires a positive value. Alternatives to Einstein's theory have also been tried. Brans–Dicke theory was left very little room to differ from general relativity, and the analysis of GW170817 ruled out many alternatives.

And the lesson? Einstein published a wrong equation in October 1915, then fixed it. Later he added Λ and removed it, yet the debate over it is still alive today. Mistakes are part of science. The real requirement is that every idea be tested, however beautiful it may be. Einstein's theory proved strong because its predictions were tested against observations again and again. So the next time you see an image of a black hole, remember that the big turning point of this journey came on 25 November 1915. What do you think the next big question in physics will be? Is equation ne Mercury ke orbit ki non-Newtonian perihelion precession bhi predict kar di, aur Einstein bohat purjosh ho gaye. Lekin jald hi ek masla samne aaya. Yeh equations energy aur momentum ki local conservation ke sath tab hi chalti thin jab poori kainat mein mass-energy ki density ek jaisi ho. Yani hawa, pathar aur khali vacuum, sab ki density barabar! To Einstein ko kya karna para? Phir 25 November 1915 ko unhon ne Prussian Academy of Sciences ke samne kya pesh kiya? shorts.titleEn: The Eclipses That Could Have Ruined Einstein
shorts.text: اگر 1912 اور 1914 میں موسم صاف ہوتا، تو شاید Einstein کی prediction غلط ثابت ہو جاتی! 1911 میں Einstein نے کہا تھا کہ سورج کے کنارے پر starlight کا deflection 0.83 seconds of arc ہوگا۔ Astronomers کو یہ سورج گرہن میں جانچنا تھا۔ 1912 میں Charles Perrine کی team نے Brazil میں اس کے لیے خاص equipment بنایا، مگر torrential rains نے تمام observations روک دیں۔ پھر 21 August 1914 کے eclipse کے لیے تین expeditions Crimea پہنچیں۔ مگر First World War شروع ہو چکی تھی، اور German astronomers کو یا تو واپس جانا پڑا یا Russians نے انہیں پکڑ لیا۔ باقی astronomers کے لیے clouds رکاوٹ بن گئے۔ بعد میں پتا چلا کہ 0.83 کی value، correct value سے factor of two کم تھی۔ تو 1915 میں Einstein نے کون سا نیا number دیا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Agar 1912 aur 1914 mein mausam saaf hota, to shayad Einstein ki prediction ghalat sabit ho jati! 1911 mein Einstein ne kaha tha ke suraj ke kinare par starlight ka deflection 0.83 seconds of arc hoga. Astronomers ko yeh suraj grahan mein jaanchna tha. 1912 mein Charles Perrine ki team ne Brazil mein is ke liye khas equipment banaya, magar torrential rains ne tamam observations rok diye. Phir 21 August 1914 ke eclipse ke liye teen expeditions Crimea pohanchin. Magar First World War shuru ho chuki thi, aur German astronomers ko ya to wapas jana para ya Russians ne unhein pakar liya. Baqi astronomers ke liye clouds rukawat ban gaye. Baad mein pata chala ke 0.83 ki value, correct value se factor of two kam thi. To 1915 mein Einstein ne kaun sa naya number diya? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Eclipse expeditions in 1912 and 1914 were stopped by rain, clouds and the outbreak of war.
Had they succeeded, Einstein's 1911 prediction of 0.83 arcseconds might have been disproved.

shorts.titleEn: The Quaker Astronomer Who Tested Einstein
shorts.text: ایک Quaker astronomer کو فوج کے بجائے eclipse expedition کیوں ملی؟ 1916 میں جنگ جاری تھی اور Arthur Eddington کو Einstein کے papers ملے، جو neutral Dutch physicist Willem de Sitter نے Royal Astronomical Society کو بھیجے تھے۔ Eddington نے theory کی اہمیت سمجھ لی اور کہا کہ eclipse observations جیسے tests ضروری ہیں۔ Astronomer Royal Frank Watson Dyson نے May 1919 کے eclipse کی planning شروع کی۔ 1917 میں Britain میں conscription شروع ہوئی۔ Eddington Quaker تھے، اور انہوں نے religious grounds پر conscientious objector ہونے کا موقف رکھا۔ June اور July 1918 کی hearings میں Dyson نے تجویز دی کہ Eddington 1919 کے eclipse پر Einstein کی theory کو test کریں۔ Board نے بارہ مہینے کی extension دے دی۔ پھر November 1918 میں Armistice ہو گیا۔ تو کیا expedition پھر بھی ہوئی؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Ek Quaker astronomer ko fauj ke bajaye eclipse expedition kyun mili? 1916 mein jang jari thi aur Arthur Eddington ko Einstein ke papers milay, jo neutral Dutch physicist Willem de Sitter ne Royal Astronomical Society ko bheje thay. Eddington ne theory ki ahmiyat samajh li aur kaha ke eclipse observations jaise tests zaroori hain. Astronomer Royal Frank Watson Dyson ne May 1919 ke eclipse ki planning shuru ki. 1917 mein Britain mein conscription shuru hui. Eddington Quaker thay, aur unhon ne religious grounds par conscientious objector hone ka mauqif rakha. June aur July 1918 ki hearings mein Dyson ne tajweez di ke Eddington 1919 ke eclipse par Einstein ki theory ko test karein. Board ne barah mahine ki extension de di. Phir November 1918 mein Armistice ho gaya. To kya expedition phir bhi hui? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
Arthur Eddington, a Quaker and conscientious objector, was given a year's extension to test Einstein's theory at the 1919 eclipse.
The Armistice came in November 1918, but the expedition went ahead.
